title: Research Program: Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – MOLECULAR AND CELLULAR ONCOGENESIS PROGRAM The Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis (MCO) Program at the Wistar Cancer Center consists of fifteen members, all engaged in a broad continuum of basic, translational, and patient-oriented cancer research. The overarching goal of the MCO Program builds on its unique culture of collaboration, uniting a multidisciplinary array of high-end approaches to improve the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. The targeted recruitment of new Program members combined with a strategic realignment of Cancer Center Programs in the last five years have added new research depth in basic and translational cancer biology and considerably strengthened the three flagship research themes of the MCO Program in (i) targeted cancer therapeutics; (ii) cancer metabolism; and (iii) the immune microenvironment. Woven into the fabric of the three flagship themes are two areas of horizontal intra-programmatic collaboration in medicinal chemistry and systems biology, creating a strong foundation in discovery medicine to fulfill the Program’s overarching mission. Rated Exceptional to Outstanding at the 2018 Cancer Center Support Grant (CCSG) renewal, the MCO Program under the leadership of Murphy (MCO Program Leader) and Liang (MCO Program co-Leader) has now increased its total funding base from $4,631,410 to $5,560,508 (a 17% increase) and peer-reviewed cancer-related funding from $3,415,520 to $4,349,733 (a 22% increase). NCI funding currently stands at $3,690,631 translating into an exceptional cancer focus of the Program of 85%. Transdisciplinary collaboration is a hallmark of the MCO Program. Accordingly, an exceptional 94% of cancer-related peer-reviewed funding ($4,081,730) originates from internal and external collaborations, and 50% of our 231 cancer-related discovery articles are collaborative, with 26% and 43% as intra- and inter-programmatic collaborations, respectively. Reflecting its deep-rooted culture of collaboration, the MCO Program of 2025 is home to impactful multi-investigator and trans-institutional awards, including the only Specialized Program of Research Excellence (SPORE) in melanoma and skin cancer of the region (PI, Herlyn; P50 CA261608), a program project grant on melanoma targeted therapies (PI, Herlyn; P01 CA114046), a consortium grant on high-throughput melanoma drug discovery using patient-derived xenograft models (PI, Villanueva; U54 CA224070), and 21 collaborative R01 grants (19 from the NCI, 90%). In addition, MCO Program members lead a broad portfolio of initiatives in cancer education, training and mentoring of junior investigators to become leaders in cancer research. Building on this exceptional track record of collaborative achievements, the MCO Program is poised to expand its role as a multidisciplinary catalyst of basic and translational cancer research, enabling the historic expansion of the Cancer Center during the next CCSG budget period in partnership with the Genome Regulation and Cell Signaling (GRCS) Program, and the newly launched, cancer- focused Center for Advanced Therapeutics.

title: Architecture and function of the neural crest genome
text:
Congenital disabilites are often linked to defects on the development of the neural crest, a group of migratory
stem cells that give rise to the craniofacial skeleton. Studying the molecular mechanisms controlling the formation
of these cells can reveal the genetic causes of craniofacial diseases. This knowledge can improve diagnosis,
treatments, and guide stem cell differentiation for the development of new therapeutic strategies.

title: Examining Longitudinal Changes in Accelerometer-Measured Physical Activity in Preventing Cardiovascular Disease with Novel Function Data Analysis Approaches
text:
In this project we propose to examine the role of longitudinal changes in physical activity
(PA) diurnal patterns in the prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD). To this end we will
conduct a comprehensive analysis on longitudinal data from the Women’s Health Initiative
Strong & Healthy (WHISH) accelerometry substudy with a novel functional data analysis
approach based on Riemann manifold model.

title: Modulating the DNA Damage Repair System in Traumatic Optic Neuropathy
text:
This research aims to develop new therapeutic strategies for traumatic optic neuropathy (TON), a condition
that currently has no effective treatments and leads to irreversible vision loss. By investigating the role of DNA
damage response pathways in retinal ganglion cell survival, this work seeks to uncover novel mechanisms of
neuroprotection that can be applied to TON as well as other optic neuropathies. This aligns with the National
Eye Institute's (NEI) strategic goal to drive innovative vision neuroscience with the ultimate goal of reducing
disability through improved visual outcomes.

title: Design and optimization of high refractive index proteins for deep tissue imaging in living biological systems
text:
Live tissue imaging is limited by light scattering, restricting the depth and resolution of optical microscopy. This
technology project proposes to overcome this barrier by developing and delivering novel high refractive index
proteins to living tissues, enabling deeper, high-resolution in vivo imaging. Success will transform biomedical
research by allowing real-time visualization of complex biological processes, advancing our understanding of
development and disease.

title: Mapping Mechanosensory Circuits from the Bladder to Barrington's Nucleus
text:
We will determine how the brain integrates bladder signals to control urination, which will provide
conceptual advances in understanding bladder interoception – the sensation of internal stimuli –
and its role in shaping behavior. The proposed research is a critical first step to developing
fundamental knowledge about the signals from the lower urinary tract (LUT) that can increase or
decrease the urge to urinate. This may yield improved pharmacologic and therapeutic approaches
to help the many individuals who suffer from LUT disorders prevalent with normal aging, or with
urinary tract infections, brain or spinal cord injury, and also a host of neuropsychiatric and
neurodegenerative disorders such as Multiple Sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s
disease.

title: Precision Targeting of CD1-Restricted iNKT Cells for Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
We propose studies of methods for activating and controlling the functions of a class of specialized
lymphocytes known as invariant Natural Killer T (iNKT) cells. The proposed work is strongly focused on
understanding the signals that regulate immune responses by these cells, with the overarching goal of
developing new approaches for immunotherapy of cancer.

title: Identifying and addressing missingness and bias to enhance discovery from multimodal health data
text: Increases in computational power and data availability have facilitated the development of advanced statistical methods and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, powerful tools for knowledge discovery and facilitating clinical decision making, but have also revealed limitations and across-subpopulation inconsistencies, both implicit and explicit, in both data and models. As such, robustness, safety, interpretability, and reproducibility are among several emerging areas in need of research both in computer science and biomedical informatics. This project will focus on developing a novel evaluation metric and new machine learning techniques for real-time clinical decision support in the critical care and ICU settings, with a particular focus on algorithms designed to appropriately handle missingness and bias in clinical data.

title: Sequence-specific Hybridization Capture to Reveal the lncRNA Interactome in Prostate Cancer
text:
This competitive renewal proposal is focused on the development and application of new tools to reveal
molecular signatures of non-coding RNAs and their interactors in prostate cancer. We will determine if these
signatures differ significantly in aggressive versus indolent prostate cancer, enabling new types of biomarkers
and novel mechanistic insights to guide prostate cancer diagnosis and therapy.

title: Recombination pathway and partner choices during meiosis
text:
Accurate chromosome segregation and repair of DNA breaks during sperm and egg development are essential
for preventing infertility, miscarriages, birth defects, and cancer. Developing sperm and eggs accomplish this
through specific exchanges of DNA, called recombination events. The proposed research will reveal the
mechanisms of these recombination events to increase understanding of fundamental processes critical to
human health.

title: Understanding prion-mediated transcriptional modifications and cellular phenotypes: insights into the role of Swi1 prion and prion-like behaviors of BAF proteins
text:
This project focuses on prion-based behaviors of components within the chromatin remodeling complexes -
SWI/SNF (SWItch/Sucrose Non-Fermentable) in yeast and BAF (BRG1- or BRM-Associated Factor complex) in
humans. The research will provide mechanistic insights into prion-conferred transcriptomic modifications and
phenotypes. It will also characterize prion-like activities of BAF proteins and their mutants linked to cancers and
neurological diseases.

title: Chemical proteomics strategies for quantifying inflammatory protein networks and modifications
text:
This study will develop cutting-edge proteomics strategies to enhance our understanding of dysregulated
inflammation caused by environmental and external agents. We anticipate that our research, aimed at identifying
potential new drug targets to combat inflammation, will likely provide fundamental insights into immune signaling
relevant to a broad array of inflammatory diseases.

title: Targeting Epigenetic Vulnerabilities in Osteosarcoma to Enhanced Immunotherapy
text:
The primary objective of this project is to transform the pharmacological treatment landscape for osteosarcoma
(OS) patients. Initially, we aim to elucidate the role of peptide-MHC-I epigenetic regulators through an in vitro co-
culture system and a syngeneic orthotopic mouse model. Subsequently, we will evaluate the combined effect of
acid-resistant immunocytokine therapy and the inactivation of these epigenetic modifiers in syngeneic and
CD34+ humanized mouse models, targeting the epigenetic mechanisms that facilitate OS immune evasion, with
the ultimate goal of clinical application.

title: Anti-NMDA Receptor Antibodies in Adult Brain Dysfunction: Lessons from Lupus
text:
This is a continuation of a very productive program to study neuropsychiatric manifestations of
Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, cognitive impairment, anxiety, depression and fatigue, and to
model the human disease in mice to permit a cellular and molecular characterization of brain
dysfunction.

title: Stress sensing by polycystin proteins
text:
Mechanotransduction is the process by which mechanical signals are converted into signaling pathways for
cells and organs to respond to environmental cues. The processes by which excessive cellular stretch
transmitted by intracellular calcium signaling pathways is not understood. Understanding these processes are
critical in maintaining homeostasis in cells.

title: Computational volumetric one-photon voltage imaging in rodents
text:
The brain processes information through the collective activity of large networks of neurons that integrate
incoming stimuli and respond by sending precisely timed electrical impulses towards their neighbors. Here we
propose to develop a novel computational microscopy method designed to capture the signals emitted from
fluorescent voltage-sensing reporter proteins across large volumes of mammalian brain tissue and thus measure
electrical neuronal activity from thousands of individual neurons. This unprecedented recording capacity will
enable precision studies of how neuronal network activity works on a fundamental level and will allow insights
into how it is altered in pathological disorders of the human brain.

title: Nucleus accumbens fast-spiking interneurons regulate opioid reward and addiction
text:
Identifying and understanding biological factors that promote opioid abuse and addiction can inform the
development of novel therapeutic neuromodulation strategies that help combat the opioid epidemic. The
proposed studies will test the hypothesis that fast-spiking interneurons in the nucleus accumbens represent
a powerful modulator of motivational behaviors disrupted in addiction. Identifying novel circuits that can be
harnessed to prevent and treat opioid use disorders is relevant to the NIH and NIDAs mission to tackle the
opioid abuse epidemic.

title: Novel OrganoPET Assay for Precision Therapy of Head and Neck Cancer
text:
Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCCs) are an aggressive form of cancer which are difficult to
treat due to the complexity and heterogeneity of the tumors among patients. Here we aim to develop a highly
reliable cancer modeling approach with patient-derived tumor organoids of HNSSC, screen them with clinical
radiotracers and compare with patient data from the clinic. This strategy will allow us to measure the sensitivity
to standard-of-care treatments for individual HNSCC subtypes based on their epigenetic signatures and pave a
way to develop an effective and precision therapy for HNSCC treatment.

title: Regulation of STAT3 phosphorylation and its role in orienting myocyte hypertrophy
text:
Heart failure is the most frequent cause of death in the developed world and often identified by
significant enlargement of the heart called hypertrophy. This hypertrophy is divided into early, adaptive and
chronic, disease causing stages with little knowledge to the mechanisms which regulate this transition over
time. This study proposes to identify those mechanisms and therapeutically promote the persistence of
adaptive hypertrophy which associates with significantly greater heart performance.

title: Role of Prp protease in the S. pneumoniae ribosome
text:
Streptococcus pneumoniae is an important human pathogen, and the increased incidence of antibiotic
resistance is a significant public health concern. The ribosome is a central organelle in all bacteria and
a key target for antibiotics. This project addresses a previously undescribed processing step in the
streptococcal ribosome that may play a role in antibiotic resistance and survival under stress conditions,
and may lead to the development of novel therapeutic approaches that target this step.
